sources.news_title: Why Does Donald Trump Forbid Access to the White House to CNN and Other Media?
MAGA Turns on Trump Over Wild Media Ban
sources.text:
Some of Donald Trump’s most ardent defenders have lashed out at the president’s bid to ban media from the White House, describing the move as a desperate bid to get more favorable coverage—and warning it could backfire spectacularly.
As his popularity continues to tank in the polls, the president on Friday announced that CNN, MS NOW, and Politico would be barred from the White House, and suggested that other outlets such as The New York Times and The Washington Post could be next.
The announcement represented another escalation in the president’s extraordinary second-term campaign to punish news organizations he believes are insufficiently friendly to his administration.
However, the 80-year-old’s latest chilling threat to the First Amendment appears to have unnerved even some of Trump’s conservative and MAGA allies.
Conservative legal scholar Jonathan Turley, a longstanding defender of the president, said the move was an “assault on long-honored principles of a free press,” while acknowledging that he has frequently criticized left-leaning outlets for bias.
“Barring disfavored media from the White House is a terrible precedent and practice,” Turley wrote, warning that it raises “serious constitutional questions.”
“It is hard for the United States to advocate for press rights globally when it is banning disfavored outlets,” he added.
Fox News anchor Brit Hume reposted Turley’s criticism with a blunt warning: “100%. And if he thinks this will lead to more favorable coverage, I think he’s dreaming,” he said.
Consultant and former George W. Bush press secretary Ari Fleischer agreed that some outlets were biased—but argued the answer was to challenge them, not restrict them.
“Open the pool and the briefing room to conservatives. Challenge liberal reporters. Argue and defeat them. Don’t ban them. Or one day they’ll ban us,” Fleischer said.
Even Trump loyalist Laura Loomer turned the dispute into a complaint about her own exclusion, arguing that the White House had mishandled press credentials for pro-Trump independent journalists while allowing “hostile” reporters access.
“I hate to say it, but in a way, the White House created this issue when they decided to deny certain independent journalists who have always supported the President press passes while allowing for hostile media to get front-row access during every press briefing,” the MAGA acolyte said.
“I love President Trump, but his staff should have seen this coming when they treated anti-Trump media personalities so well and bent over backwards to reward Trump haters in the fake news media,” Loomer added.
Trump’s announcement came after a brutal stretch of news, including polls showing his approval deeply underwater over the Iran war and affordability, a federal court ruling blocking his attempt to put his name back on the Kennedy Center, and fresh setbacks over his administration’s attempt to control mail-in voting.
Moments before he announced his ban, Politico also published an extraordinary report that sensitive F-35 components being shipped from Australia to the U.S. were diverted to Hong Kong and went missing, raising concerns that China could potentially gain access to stealth technology.
The Pentagon confirmed a “shipment issue” and said it was working to recover the parts; there is no public confirmation that China obtained them.
Against the backdrop of a tough week, and merely 45 days from the midterms, Trump’s instinct was not to change the news, but to attempt to change who gets to report it.
“There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” he told reporters after announcing his ban on Truth Social, claiming it would be “effective immediately.”
“Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine. But I don’t have to let them into my…,” he added, before correcting himself, “into the People’s House.”
The legal fight could be familiar territory for Trump. In 2018, his White House revoked then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s press pass after a heated exchange with the president.
CNN sued, arguing the move violated Acosta’s constitutional rights, and a federal judge ordered the White House to restore his credentials. The administration ultimately backed down.
Asked what might be different this time, Trump told reporters it would “depend on the judge.” But some legal experts don’t believe the ban would hold up in court, while others described it as yet another “distraction.”
What Trump’s ban would mean in practice is also unclear, as his aides did not immediately provide clarity.
Asked if he thought Trump would follow through, Ty Cobb, the president’s former lawyer, told CNN on Friday: “We know that he thinks it’s his house. He leveled the East Wing in violation of the law and without talking to Congress; he has gilded the Oval Office with so much gold you have to wear sunglasses in there just to avoid the wh**ehouse vibes… Let’s not put anything past him.”
Trump’s announcement on Friday was the latest attempt to undermine the free press. Last year, the White House restricted AP reporters from presidential events after AP refused to call the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America”.
Trump has also cut funding to NPR and PBS, threatened to revoke the broadcast licenses of ABC, NBC, and CNN after they declined to carry one of his prime-time speeches live, and has repeatedly attacked female reporters with vile insults.
Fox News reporter Jacqui Heinrich, the president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, said, “This is about more than the rights of journalists. It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.”

NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles!
President Donald Trump announced Friday that CNN, MS NOW and Politico will be banned from the White House.
“I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW … and Politico … from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
Trump doubled down on his announced ban while taking questions from reporters at the Oval Office, citing “cumulative stories” the three outlets have published over the years.
“You get sick of it,” Trump said.
CNN FIRES BACK AT TRUMP WHITE HOUSE OVER ATTACKS ON REPORTER, CALLS THEM ‘BENEATH THE OFFICE’
Trump denied he was trying to intimidate the press from doing its job in an exchange with another reporter.
For decades, CNN has been part of a rotating pool of five networks, including Fox News, that travel with the president around the world.
Notably, CNN has already been selected to lead network pool coverage Monday as Trump is set to attend the United Nations General Assembly.
TRUMP BLASTS NEW YORK TIMES, CNN FOR ‘SEDITIOUS’ COVERAGE OF IRAN WAR
Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the Republican Arkansas governor and former White House press secretary during the first Trump administration, was in attendance at the Oval Office event focused on healthcare and rejected the notion that Trump opposes a free press that’s enshrined in the First Amendment of the Constitution.
“I think it’s hard for you to argue against a free press when you’re literally standing in the Oval Office asking questions of the president of the United States,” Sanders told reporters. “He has been more accessible and easier to talk to than any president in history.”
CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS
Past efforts by the Trump administration to ban outlets and individual journalists have been blocked by federal judges.
“I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day, after day, after day. I think that somebody has a right to keep them away,” Trump said.
Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy said CNN was still broadcasting live from their tent on the media row outside the White House, but a senior White House official told him that the top brass at CNN, MS NOW and Politico were being informed that their journalists cannot come to the White House grounds beginning Saturday.
“CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” the network said in a statement on X. “We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right.”
Politico also issued a statement, telling Fox News Digital, “Politico will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them.”
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A spokesperson for MS NOW declined to comment.

In the move that will finally, conclusively stop people from saying bad things about him—like that he’s a thin-skinned, petulant attention addict obsessed with what people he claims to hate say about him—Donald Trump issued a statement today that he’s banning CNN, MSNOW, and Politico from the White House. At last: The Problem With Journalists, solved.
  
Trump made these statements, obviously, on his own Truth Social social media platform, your go-to online stop for official pronouncements that the United States is, like, annexing Greenland, mixed with ads for your preferred brands of horse dewormer. Promising “other fake news media outlets to follow,” Trump claimed to have banned the three named organizations from the White House, although he didn’t go into further details about what the practicalities of the ban, an upending of years of press pool precedence, would look like. 
  
This isn’t the first time Trump has moved to cut access to outlets he’s decided to make an example of, most notably banning The Associated Press from the Oval Office and other more select press opportunities last year over its refusal to bend the knee and start calling the Gulf Of Mexico the Gulf Of America. (The AP sued, and a judge issued an initial order letting them back into those room, but a Trump-friendly appeals judge put a stay on that order until the court case is resolved.) This latest pronouncement/tantrum is quite a bit more sweeping, though, hitting multiple outlets at once for their vaguely outlined crimes against the administration. (In a press conference later on Friday, Trump also highlighted The New York Times and The Washington Post as outlets he might consider “throwing out,” which we have to assume hurt poor Jeff Bezos’ “But I Complied In Advance!” feelings.)
CNN’s own reporting on the “ban” makes it clear that it hasn’t heard from Trump and his team about how they intend to actually enforce what is, at the moment, really just a social media post on a social media network that feels like it’s one bad pop-up ad from giving our antivirus software an aneurysm; the network put out a statement today asserting that “CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting. We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right.”

sources.news_title: Trump bans CNN, MSNOW, and Politico from White House: ‘Reporting FAKE NEWS’, ‘They write fiction and lies’
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump on Friday (September 18), announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be barred from the White House, accusing the three news organisations of repeatedly publishing what he called “fake news.”
Trump made the announcement on his Truth Social platform and warned that other media outlets could face similar restrictions.
“I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW... and Politico... from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” Trump wrote.
The White House did not immediately provide details on how the ban would be implemented or whether it would affect press credentials, briefings, presidential events or the White House press pool.
Trump did not identify specific reports that prompted the decision. He said news organisations should not be allowed to publish what he considers false information about his administration.
“Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” Trump wrote.
“Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added.
Later, speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump defended his decision, saying he believed the president had the right to exclude outlets that “write false stories all the time.”
The announcement immediately raised questions over the constitutional limits of the president's authority to restrict access to the White House based on news coverage.
The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press said a ban based on an outlet's coverage would be unconstitutional. Its president, Bruce D. Brown, said: “A ban like this would be flatly unconstitutional.”
The First Amendment protects freedom of the press, but the legal question surrounding White House access can involve distinctions between general access to government officials and access to limited-capacity events or spaces.
Trump's announcement is therefore likely to trigger legal and press-freedom challenges.
Trump has also pursued legal action against several other major news organisations during his second term.
The latest action follows Trump's decision in 2025 to restrict Associated Press journalists from certain White House events after the news agency continued using “Gulf of Mexico” rather than Trump's preferred “Gulf of America.”
The AP challenged the restrictions in court. Trump has also pursued legal action against several other major news organisations during his second term.
The administration has separately tightened rules governing which journalists participate in press pools covering the president in restricted spaces.
Trump's warning that “other Fake News Media Outlets” could follow CNN, MS NOW and Politico adds another dimension to Friday's announcement.
However, he did not identify which organisations could be targeted next, nor did the White House immediately explain how the restrictions would work.
The move marks another escalation in Trump's long-running conflict with news organisations whose coverage he considers unfavorable.

sources.news_title: The Latest: Trump says he is banning CNN, MSNOW and Politico from White House over their coverage
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Friday that he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House due to what he called unfavorable coverage, and threatened that more such prohibitions of media outlets could follow.
Meanwhile, in-person voting for this year’s midterm elections is underway in Virginia, ushering in the final six weeks for Americans to decide which party they trust to lead Congress at a time of a cost-of-living crisis, a prolonged war in Iran and other pressing issues. Voters in Idaho, Minnesota and South Dakota, can cast absentee ballots in person.
And a top official at the U.S. Postal Service has said the agency has stopped work on developing a controversial computer system that was central to Trump’s effort to limit mail voting after the Supreme Court rejected his executive order this week.
Here's the latest:
Ban on selling handguns to adults under 21 is unconstitutional, Justice Department says
Federal law banning licensed firearms dealers from selling to them is unconstitutional and can’t be enforced, the department said in a legal opinion released Friday.
The opinion from the DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel said the law, aimed at making it harder for 18- to 20-year-olds to get handguns, violates the Second Amendment.
The opinion indicates that the Trump administration will not defend or prosecute cases under the law, which has been the subject of competing court rulings in the wake of a landmark Supreme Court decision that transformed the legal landscape.
Federal appeals courts have split on whether handgun age limits are constitutional, and the U.S. Supreme Court has yet to weigh in on the federal law in the wake of the 2022 landmark decision that changed the test used to evaluate challenges to firearm restrictions.
Gun control groups called the Justice Department’s opinion misguided and dangerous.
Judge rules EPA illegally terminated $7 billion solar program intended to help poorer Americans
The Trump administration illegally terminated the Solar for All program, designed to make solar power accessible to more than 900,000 lower-income people, the federal judge in Rhode Island ruled Friday.
The Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the Solar for All funds in August 2025 after Trump’s massive tax and spending law passed in Congress. Administrator Lee Zeldin called the Biden-era grant program a “boondoggle.”
District Judge Mary McElroy wrote in the ruling that Congress clearly intended the EPA to continue administering the Solar for All grants that were already obligated. The EPA acted contrary to this intent and without any other statutory authority, McElroy said, and she vacated the termination.
The EPA said it was reviewing the decision and considering options for appeal.
The lawsuit by the Rhode Island AFL-CIO labor organization and others highlighted the importance of the program for local workforces and lower-income communities seeking access to clean-energy project funding.
Somaliland president seeks greater US recognition, offers Red Sea access
In return the leader of the breakaway Somali republic is floating the potential of military and commercial access to the territory’s Gulf of Aden coast.
After concluding various meetings with U.S. officials and lawmakers, President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi said Friday that establishing a U.S. diplomatic post in the capital of Hargeisa or the city of Berbera, a major port near the entrance to the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that has played a critical role in the Iran war, is a priority for his government.
A number of lawmakers have called for the Trump administration to recognize Somaliland as an independent country, particularly after Israel did so earlier this year.
While the administration has stepped up ties with Somaliland — providing it with $6.2 million in counterterrorism, security and humanitarian assistance — it continues to recognize the territorial integrity of Somalia, which includes Somaliland.
Trump administration begins building border wall in West Texas’ Big Bend region
It is the first major construction in an area of the U.S.-Mexico border where the administration’s plans have met with heavy opposition.
The start of construction marks a milestone in the administration’s $46 billion plan to line the border with walls, barriers, roads and technology. Customs and Border Protection says it has doubled the pace of building.
CBP said in a statement to AP that “border wall panel installation is underway” in a 47-mile stretch of Hudspeth County known as Big Bend 1. There are a total of five project areas that make up the roughly 500-mile Big Bend region, stretching from an area of Hudspeth County south of El Paso to Lake Amistad.
The agency said the first panels were erected Sept. 15. On the agency’s website a photo shows a crane lifting one of the 30-foot tall steel wall panels into place.
In the broader Big Bend region, CBP has run up against opposition from landowners, environmental groups, business owners and ranchers who say the remote area is not a high-traffic area for illegal immigration.
Greenland deal looks similar to previous one but comes at a steep diplomatic cost, expert says
Greenland and Denmark “were always willing to consider an expanded U.S. military presence,” said Imran Bayoumi, an associate director at the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security.
“They were always looking to potentially grow that military presence as well as welcome U.S. investment in a variety of sectors,” he added.
But Trump’s repeated demands for Greenland and threats to take it by force rattled the NATO alliance and discomfited European allies, Bayoumi said.
“I think Americans really underestimate how damaging it was for the image of the United States in Europe,” he said. “I think Greenlanders, Danes, Europeans saw this as a real attack on their sovereignty, and it’s going to take a lot of work to repair.”
US officials say Washington and Beijing may be ready to ease some tariffs on some nonstrategic goods
Speaking on a call with reporters, senior officials said there have been discussions ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington about reducing certain tariffs in nonstrategic sectors.
The officials, who insisted on anonymity as ground rules to hold the call, said such a move might affect a narrow band of goods that would advantage both sides. They did not elaborate.
The officials do not expect the U.S. to be ready to ease export controls to allow for greater flow of rare earth minerals into the global market.
They said China maintaining an acceptable flow of such minerals would be discussed but there is unlikely to be an exchange involving reduced U.S. export controls.
— Will Weissert
Trump administration official suggests Iran war won’t dominate UN General Assembly agenda
A senior Trump administration official says Iran will be a key discussion topic at the annual gathering but stressed that it won’t be the only topic.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House, said artificial intelligence will also be a focus.
A meeting focused on the governance of AI is to be led by France’s foreign minister.
The official said a G20 meeting on Ebola and the administration’s response to the crisis in parts of Africa is also on the schedule. The official said other discussions will cover undersea cables and seabed minerals.
— Darlene Superville
US removes Eritrea sanctions imposed over conflict with Ethiopia
The Trump administration lifted a broad swath of sanctions against the Eritrean government, armed forces and certain senior officials, allowing penalties imposed in 2021 to expire as the Horn of Africa nation becomes potentially important in securing Red Sea shipping while the U.S.-Iran war drags on.
The Treasury Department said Friday in a notice that it allowed an executive order signed by former President Joe Biden during the height of a conflict between Eritrea and neighboring Ethiopia to lapse.
In addition to six individuals, two companies and the country’s main political party, which controls the government, the step removes U.S. sanctions from the Eritrean Defense Forces.
Trump defends bid to put his name on the Kennedy Center
The president said he deserves recognition for trying to save it and claimed that he could secure the $257 million Congress approved for repairs. He also suggested that the center requires an ongoing subsidy to stay open.
A judge recently blocked plans to return Trump’s name to the building and ordered 30 days’ notice before any major changes.
Trump called the judge “hostile.”
The Kennedy Center board, aligned with Trump, voted to close the center indefinitely for repairs.
Artists canceled appearances after the board added his name to the facade.
White House announces schedule for Chinese president’s state visit
Trump will greet Xi Jinping and his wife, Madame Peng, on Wednesday at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.
The next day the president and first lady Melania Trump will welcome the couple at an arrival ceremony on the State Floor of the White House.
The leaders will participate in a military review in the Rose Garden before their closed-door meeting. The first lady and Madame Peng will follow a separate schedule.
Xi and Madame Peng will also be the guests of honor at a state dinner Thursday in the East Room.
Xi and his wife return to the White House on Friday morning for tea with the Trumps, who will then take them on a tour of the National Archives, home to some of the United States’ most important documents.
Xi will return to Joint Base Andrews.
Rubio hails accord with Denmark and Greenland, says US interests will be forever protected
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the agreement reached to permanently maintain an American military presence on the island is a historic win that will secure U.S. interests in that part of the Arctic.
“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” Rubio said in a statement. “This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland.”
The State Department said following Trump’s announcement of the deal that it will allow the U.S. to increase the number of bases it has in Greenland at will.
Greenland, which is a territory of Denmark, was already covered by NATO defense guarantees and previously hosted U.S. military facilities, although there was no proscription against non-NATO members establishing bases there.
Several top CEOs attending China state dinner
There won’t be a shortage of tech power at Trump’s state dinner honoring Xi Jinping next week.
Among the executives scheduled to attend are Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai of Google and Michael Dell, CEO of Dell Technologies.
Also on the invite list are Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Jane Fraser, CEO of Citigroup, and Tim Cook, who recently left his position as CEO of Apple.
Trump announces all 50 states joining Medicaid drug pricing model
The president said every state will join the program set to provide Most Favored Nation pricing to some drugs within the Medicaid program, bringing the net price of selected drugs down to prices paid in certain other countries.
The administration claims that Medicaid will save billions on prescription drug costs as a result of the plan, dubbed the Medicaid “GENEROUS” model. Experts say the savings are unclear since the content of the deals isn’t public.
Cost-of-living issues are at the forefront of voters’ concerns ahead of the midterms. In a way to address affordability concerns, Trump has cut deals with pharmaceutical companies so that the cost of some drugs in the U.S. would not be dramatically higher than in other affluent nations.
But critics say his administration has not presented a viable plan for broadly addressing rising health costs, especially after Republicans let Affordable Care Act subsidies expire this year, sending plan costs soaring.
Trump to meet acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez in New York next week, White House says
The president has several meetings scheduled with other world leaders while he is in New York City for the United Nations General Assembly next week.
He will participate in a “pull-aside” meeting — a more casual meeting than a formal bilateral sit-down — with acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez, according to Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations.
Waltz also told reporters on a Friday call that Trump will be meeting with Andy Burnham, the United Kingdom prime minister, and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Trump also will meet with leaders of the Gulf Cooperation Council.
Denmark says Greenland deal to be signed next week, still needs parliamentary action
The office of Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the Greenland deal with the U.S. will be signed by three governments next week during the United Nations General Assembly. However parliamentary action is still needed by the Danish and Greenland governments before it can be enforced.
Frederiksen said in a statement that “the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity” of Greenland and Denmark and upholds both people’s right “to self-determination.”
Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions bill, aiming to choke off funds for Moscow in Ukraine war
The sweeping sanctions package targets Russian officials and key pillars of its economy and is meant to punish and pressure Moscow for the ongoing war against Ukraine.
The measure was a final legacy item for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., a close ally and friend of the president who had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. In the works for more than a year, the bill passed with large bipartisan margins: 86-11 in the Senate and 262-159 in the House.
It is meant to starve President Vladimir Putin of the resources Russia needs to continue the war after invading Ukraine more than four years ago. The bill sanctions officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.
It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for some countries.
Trump disagrees with Republican lawmaker’s ad against his immigration policy
In a new campaign ad, Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar breaks with the president on immigration and says some of his enforcement efforts have “gone too far.”
Salazar represents a majority Hispanic district in South Florida and is in a competitive race for reelection in November. Trump endorsed her in the primary.
Asked if he still supports Salazar and had seen the video, Trump said, “I do and I have.”
He added, “I disagree with her.”
“I’m very strong on the borders,” Trump said, “and she isn’t.”
Media organizations on White House ban announcement from Trump
CNN denounced the move, saying it stands behind its White House team and their “fair and accurate reporting.”
“We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government,” it said in a statement on the social platform X. “Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right.”
Politico said it would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them.”
Trump says he has a deal with Denmark to bolster US military presence in Greenland
The president said Friday that he has a deal with Denmark to bolster the U.S. military presence in Greenland after months of threatening to take the island by force from the NATO ally.
Trump, in a social media post announcing the agreement, said it “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns.”
He added that with the agreement, his administration would “immediately” begin the process of developing a larger military presence on the mineral-rich Danish territory.
The Danish Embassy in Washington had no immediate comment.
Trump says new White House helipad opens Monday
“They’re going to have an official opening on the 21st with the first helicopter landing, etc. and it’s beautiful,” Trump said about the granite helipad on the South Lawn of the White House.
Trump designed the landing pad in the image of the presidential seal.
He has said the helipad was necessary because the new versions of the Marine One presidential helicopter are so powerful that they would burn the grass.
Trump has said Sikorsky Aircraft, a subsidiary of defense contractor Lockheed Martin, would pay for it.
The White House has not said how much it cost.
Trump says his son’s wedding celebration being partially funded by a Russian oligarch is ‘totally allowed’
Asked about Donald Trump Jr.’s recent wedding being bankrolled in part by Umar Kremlev, who has close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump said “a lot of people have parties” and “it’s totally allowed.”
The president further suggested, without evidence, that his son was in the process of paying Kremlev back.
Trump said he heard about Kremlev paying partially for the event “a little while ago” and asked his son about it. He then recalled a conversation in which he said his son responded, “I’m paying him back, Dad.”
Trump Jr. and socialite Bettina Anderson were married in the Bahamas in May. The president did not attend, suggesting that he was too busy with major issue like the war in Iran.
ProPublica first reported the story about Kremlev’s involvement this week.
Schumer slams Trump’s media ban as what dictators do
“This is a democracy,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer posted on X.
“You will not be able to manipulate the news or hide the truth.”

Trump says he’s banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House
-    Click here to listen to this article

- President Trump vowed Friday to ban CNN, MS NOW, Politico and other outlets from White House coverage, escalating his long-running campaign against mainstream media he brands “fake news.”
- The Truth Social declaration offers no details on how a ban would work; past efforts to revoke credentials, including the Jim Acosta case, have been blocked in court.
- Press freedom advocates condemned the threat as a blatant 1st Amendment violation and politically self-defeating, warning it deepens Trump’s pattern of retaliating against critical coverage.
President Trump declared Friday that he is banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House “effective immediately,” an extraordinary escalation in his ongoing feud with the news media.
The action marks the latest salvo in a campaign against the press that has already won him multimillion-dollar settlements from two networks, put ABC’s broadcast licenses under federal review and kept the Associated Press out of the Oval Office for more than a year. It also tests how far the courts will let a president go in deciding who gets to cover him.
In a statement on Truth Social, Trump attacked the reporting of the three outlets, which he described as “FAKE NEWS!”
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States of America,” Trump said.
How a ban would be enacted remains to be seen. Based on Trump’s past clashes with the press, barring the outlets from the White House is unlikely to stand up to a legal challenge. In 2018, the White House tried to ban journalist Jim Acosta, then working for CNN, but a court ordered that his press credential be restored.
It was unclear whether the ban would apply only to White House press briefings or would bar all access to the White House grounds.
Last year, the Trump White House issued a ban on the Associated Press when the news organization refused to recognize the president’s renaming of the Gulf of Mexico by executive order. A federal judge ordered that the AP’s access to the White House be restored on the grounds that the government cannot punish a journalistic outlet over the content of its speech.
An emboldened president and his allies have launched a vigorous campaign to use levers of government to intimidate an increasingly fragmented and polarized media, experts say.
A divided appeals court panel later paused that ruling for the Oval Office, Air Force One and other restricted spaces, allowing the White House to keep the AP out of them while the case proceeds.
Trump’s remarks generated an immediate outcry from press freedom groups.
“It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the 1st Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticizing the government,” Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement.
“It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move. The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him.”
Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News White House correspondent and president of the White House Correspondents’ Assn., also decried the move.
“This is about more than the rights of journalists. It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office,” Heinrich said in a statement.
Trump has stepped up his attacks on the press during his second term. Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr has threatened the broadcast licenses of outlets Trump dislikes. Carr has called for a review of ABC’s TV licenses, which the Walt Disney Co.-owned network is challenging in court.
FCC Chair Brendan Carr goes after broadcast networks as negative stories mount against the Trump administration amid Iran war.
Trump has extracted multimillion-dollar settlements from ABC and CBS after suing them over their reporting. The president also has a defamation suit against the BBC for $10 billion over a documentary on his reelection campaign that he claimed sent a “false message” that he encouraged Jan. 6 rioters.
After the Truth Social post circulated, Trump held a press briefing from the Oval Office to discuss drug pricing. According to the pool reporter covering the event, no journalist was removed from the press room.
Trump was asked about the Truth Social post. He responded by further attacking the three outlets. He did not cite any specific report that led to his call for a ban.
“I dislike dishonest press,” he said.
After a reporter pointed out that a judge restored Acosta’s credential after it was pulled by the White House, Trump indicated he’s willing to take his chances in the courts again.
“Depends on the judge you get, to be honest with you,” he said. “I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day.”
Trump said other outlets may be subjected to the ban as well. When asked how to square his pronouncement with the 1st Amendment right to a free press, Trump continued to lambaste the news organizations he cited and reiterated his general beef with outlets that do not provide fawning coverage.
Kristen Holmes, CNN’s senior White House correspondent, continued to report from the White House grounds after the ban was announced. The network did not have a reporter in the pool covering his Oval Office remarks.
“CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” the network said in a statement. “We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right.”
MS NOW declined to comment on the president’s Truth Social post. But a person familiar with the situation who was not authorized to comment publicly said MS NOW journalists were still on the White House grounds late Friday afternoon and there was no attempt to remove them.
Trump referred to the New York Times and the Washington Post as “fake news” but did not say they would be banned.
“They’re crummy papers — both doing very poorly by the way,” he said. “We’re probably not going to display those papers anymore in the White House, but we haven’t taken the step of throwing them out.”
Tim Richardson, journalism and disinformation director at PEN America, said, “Someone needs to explain to President Trump how the 1st Amendment works. ... This administration’s hostility toward the press is never about the accuracy of news stories, but about its inability to withstand scrutiny of its actions.”
Times staff writers Meg James and Michael Wilner contributed to this report.

The Associated Press has been a frequent target of the Trump administration during the president’s second term. President Donald Trump said on Friday he is banning three major news outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — from the White House in his latest move to crack down on the independent press.
The move is almost certain to face legal challenges as free speech experts said it conflicts with the Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press.
Trump accused the outlets of “reporting FAKE NEWS” in a social media post, and said they “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” Trump added, “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
Representatives of all three outlets could be seen working in the White House on Friday afternoon following Trump’s post.
In later comments to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump said there was no specific incident that prompted the ban, adding, “It’s really just cumulative stories over the past few years.”
Trump added, “I don’t have to let them into my, into the people’s house.”
The extent of the ban announced by Trump was not immediately clear, and the legality of any move could depend on its scope.
Courts have given presidents broad discretion over selective access to events such as Oval Office meetings and small press pools, while broader exclusions from generally available White House press facilities or credentials could face stronger challenges under the First Amendment and constitutional protections for due process.
Trump’s move came weeks ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections in which Trump’s fellow Republicans are defending narrow majorities in Congress. Reuters/Ipsos polls show the public souring on Republicans, as Trump’s own approval ratings stand near historic lows amid the deeply unpopular Iran war he kicked off that has sent energy prices soaring.
Decades of tradition
The Trump administration has upended decades of tradition in dealings between the White House and press, cutting back the access many major news organizations have had to the president while elevating the presence of new media outlets seen as more sympathetic to the administration.
CNN in a statement said it stands behind its journalists who cover the White House. CNN’s team remained at the White House working as if it were a normal Friday afternoon, CNN reporter Brian Stelter said on air.
“We have a right under the US Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government,” CNN said in a statement. “Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right.
MS NOW and Politico did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
“It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticizing the government,” Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement.
Jameel Jaffer, executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, said the First Amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he does not like their coverage.
“If President Trump means to expel these news organizations from the White House press pool, his action is doubly unconstitutional because the press pool is a ‘public forum’ under the First Amendment, which means the president can’t exclude journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints,” Jaffer said in a statement.
Trump rose to fame as a New York developer skilled in getting the city’s tabloid newspapers to cover his social life, and went on to build his profile as a reality television personality before making a serious push into politics.
Since his successful 2016 campaign, Trump has regularly criticized the press, stepping up his complaints during his second term in office. He has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programs he dislikes or which have joked about or criticized him or his administration, calling on the Federal Communications Commission to strip disfavored broadcast stations of their licenses.
Trump has filed several lawsuits against the press, including the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times, the BBC and the Des Moines Register. The suits can have a chilling effect. His defamation suits against ABC and CBS were settled for $15 million and $16 million, respectively.
In 2019, the White House credential of Brian Karem, a Playboy magazine correspondent, was suspended after he traded insults with Sebastian Gorka, then an aide to the president, in the White House Rose Garden. A judge later ordered the White House to reinstate Karem’s credential.
Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has openly badgered reporters, particularly from U.S. television networks.
Last year, he also banned the Associated Press from the usual pool of reporters that cover his movements because the news agency did not adopt Trump’s preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico, which Trump has instructed executive branch employees to refer to as the Gulf of America.
Rep. Frank Pallone, the lead Democrat on the House of Representatives Energy and Commerce Committee, called Trump’s action censorship.
“If Trump thinks banning media outlets from the White House will make his presidency seem less like a failure, he’s delusional,” Pallone said.

sources.news_title: FACT CHECK: Trump’s Claims On CNN, MS NOW And Politico — What Is True, What Is Misleading And What Is Unsupported
sources.text:
FACT CHECK: Trump’s Claims Against CNN, MS NOW And Politico
ZimEye Fact Check
US President Donald Trump has announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are being excluded from the White House, accusing the three organisations of repeatedly publishing what he calls “FAKE NEWS”, “FICTION” and “LIES”.
In the same post, Trump made specific factual claims about MS NOW’s rebranding and about more than US$8 million in federal payments to Politico.
Here is a sentence-by-sentence examination of the claims against available documentary evidence.
1. “I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN…”
FACT CHECK:
Trump did make the announcement — but the practical scope of the ban was initially unclear.
Trump publicly announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be barred from the White House. Reuters reported that Trump subsequently said he could extend the restrictions to other media organisations.
However, reporting following the announcement indicated that the precise mechanism of the alleged ban had not been clearly specified. Journalists from the three organisations were still present on White House grounds after Trump’s announcement.
Verdict: TRUE — regarding the announcement; implementation/scope was initially unclear.
2. “MSNOW (who recently changed their name from MSNBC due to lack of viewership and credibility!)”
FACT CHECK:
The reason given by Trump is not supported by the company’s corporate records.
MSNBC did indeed become MS NOW.
But the documentary explanation is substantially different.
Versant’s SEC filing states that MSNBC was rebranded MS NOW as part of the separation of the business from Comcast/NBCUniversal, with the rebranding announced in August 2025 and becoming effective in November 2025.
The corporate filing does not state that the reason was declining credibility.
More importantly, the same SEC filing reports that MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, had more than 14 million weekly viewers in 2024, and that it finished 2024 as the No. 2 network across all cable television networks according to Nielsen, for the seventh consecutive year.
The filing further says 2024 was one of the network’s largest audiences on record.
There are legitimate industry challenges facing cable television generally, including declining linear-TV audiences, and current MS NOW management has acknowledged those challenges. But that is different from saying MSNBC changed its name because it lacked viewers and credibility.
Verdict: FALSE/MISLEADING.
The rebrand happened, but the documented reason was the Comcast–Versant corporate separation, not lack of credibility.
3. “And Politico (The recipients of an illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription…)”
This requires separating the $8 million figure from Trump’s description of what the money represented.
FACT CHECK:
The $8 million figure has a real basis — but it was not an $8 million subscription.
Federal spending records show that federal agencies collectively spent more than $8 million on Politico products and subscriptions during fiscal year 2024. FactCheck.org found that the transactions were recorded as contracts, rather than grants or subsidies.
So there really was approximately $8 million in federal spending involving Politico in that fiscal year.
But Trump’s wording — “an $8 Million Dollar subscription” — gives the impression of one enormous payment.
That is not what the records show.
The spending consisted of purchases by multiple federal departments and agencies for Politico products, particularly Politico Pro.
Politico Pro is a professional information service providing policy monitoring, legislative information, analysis, directories and related tools.
For example, FactCheck.org found that HHS paid approximately $143,203 to renew 49 annual Politico Pro subscriptions — approximately $2,900 per subscription — while the Federal Trade Commission paid $45,378 for 14 subscriptions.
Verdict: PARTLY TRUE BUT MISLEADING.
There was more than $8 million in federal spending on Politico products in FY2024. It was not one $8 million payment for a single subscription.
4. “…an illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription…”
FACT CHECK:
There is no evidence in the cited government spending records establishing that the purchases were illegal.
The federal transactions were recorded as government contracts for services.
FactCheck.org examined the USAspending records and specifically found that the transactions were classified as contracts, not grants, loans or direct payments.
That does not automatically establish that every individual procurement decision was necessarily appropriate or economical. Government agencies can legitimately be criticised over whether they received sufficient value from contracts.
But “possibly wasteful” and “illegal” are different allegations.
The available evidence establishes that federal agencies purchased Politico products.
It does not establish Trump’s assertion that the purchases were illegal.
Verdict: UNSUBSTANTIATED.
5. “…directly from the United States Government…”
FACT CHECK:
Broadly true, but the wording obscures how the money was paid.
The money did come from federal government agencies.
USAspending records show federal agencies as the purchasers.
But there wasn’t a single White House payment to Politico.
Different departments bought Politico services independently.
In fact, the largest purchasers included agencies such as Health and Human Services, Interior and Energy.
Verdict: TRUE IN SUBSTANCE, but missing important context.
6. “…under Crooked Joe Biden…”
FACT CHECK:
The largest spending period cited by Trump was during Biden’s presidency, but the picture is more complicated.
FactCheck.org calculated that federal obligations to Politico from FY2021 through FY2024 totalled approximately $22.8 million. FY2021 also included almost four months under Donald Trump’s first presidency.
There is therefore a factual basis for saying substantial federal purchases occurred during the Biden administration.
But there is an important omitted fact:
Trump’s own first administration also purchased Politico services.
FactCheck.org found that federal spending on Politico occurred under both administrations.
So the existence of government purchases of Politico products is not unique to Biden.
Verdict: PARTLY TRUE, BUT SELECTIVE.
7. “…in order to keep them ‘alive.’”
FACT CHECK:
No evidence has been presented establishing this motive.
This is one of the most significant unsupported parts of the allegation.
The available government records establish a buyer–seller relationship:
Government agencies purchased Politico products.
They do not establish:
Government agencies purchased Politico products to prevent Politico from collapsing.
Politico’s management has said the company is supported by advertising and sponsorships and that government agencies represent only a small proportion of Politico Pro’s subscriber base. FactCheck.org reported that approximately 6% of Politico Pro’s roughly 5,000 subscribers were government employees at the time of its investigation.
The evidence therefore does not establish Trump’s claimed purpose.
Verdict: UNSUPPORTED.
8. “Seems like corruption to me!”
FACT CHECK:
This is Trump’s opinion, not an established fact.
Whether government procurement constitutes corruption requires evidence of something such as:
- an unlawful procurement process;
- bribery;
- a quid pro quo;
- fraudulent invoicing;
- improper influence;
- conflicts of interest; or
- another violation of law.
The spending records cited establish that government agencies purchased Politico services.
They do not, by themselves, establish corruption.
Politico’s own management characterised the transactions as ordinary commercial purchases made through government procurement processes.
That statement is itself an interested party’s position, rather than independent proof that every procurement was proper.
Verdict: CORRUPTION NOT ESTABLISHED BY THE EVIDENCE CITED.
9. “…from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”
FACT CHECK:
This is an allegation about journalistic performance, not a demonstrated factual finding.
Trump has repeatedly characterised coverage of his administration by these organisations as “fake news.”
But in this particular announcement, he did not identify specific articles or broadcasts that he alleged were demonstrably false.
The Washington Post reported that Trump gave no further details when asked to explain the ban.
CNN responded that it stood behind its White House team’s “fair and accurate reporting.” Politico similarly said it would continue reporting on the administration and defend its First Amendment rights.
Those responses are the organisations’ positions and do not independently prove the accuracy of their reporting.
Verdict: UNPROVEN GENERAL ALLEGATION.
10. “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES…”
FACT CHECK:
No specific evidence is provided in the post.
This is a broad assertion about the entire output of three major news organisations.
A proper factual assessment would require identifying the individual reports alleged to be false and comparing them with primary evidence.
The post does not do that.
Consequently, the statement cannot be independently established simply from the information contained in Trump’s post.
Verdict: NOT DEMONSTRATED.
11. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
FACT CHECK:
This is a stated intention, not a factual claim that can presently be verified.
Trump subsequently indicated that other media organisations could also face restrictions. Reuters reported that he said the ban could go “as far as you can.”
Whether additional outlets will actually be excluded is a future event.
Verdict: STATEMENT OF INTENT — NOT YET FACT-CHECKABLE AS AN OUTCOME.
THE BIG THREE CLAIMS
The post essentially rests on three factual propositions:
CLAIM 1: “MSNBC changed its name because nobody watches it.”
Evidence: The corporate explanation says the rebranding was connected to the Comcast/Versant separation. Versant’s SEC filing says the network had more than 14 million weekly viewers in 2024 and was the No. 2 cable network that year according to Nielsen.
Assessment: ❌ NOT SUPPORTED.
CLAIM 2: “Biden illegally gave Politico $8 million.”
Evidence: Federal agencies did spend more than $8 million on Politico products in FY2024. But the money was spent through contracts for subscriptions and professional information services. The records do not establish an illegal payment.
Assessment: ⚠️ REAL SPENDING, BUT THE CHARACTERISATION IS UNSUPPORTED.
CLAIM 3: “The government paid Politico $8 million to keep it alive.”
Evidence: The records show purchases of products/services. They do not establish that the purpose was to financially rescue Politico. Politico’s government customers represented a small proportion of its Politico Pro subscriber base.
Assessment: ❌ NO EVIDENCE ESTABLISHING THIS MOTIVE.
ZIMEYE FACT-CHECK CONCLUSION
The underlying US$8 million federal spending figure is real, but Trump’s description substantially changes what that figure represents.
The strongest documentary evidence shows that:
Politico did receive more than US$8 million through federal contracts in FY2024.
The money was paid by multiple federal agencies for Politico products and subscriptions.
The transactions were recorded as contracts, rather than government grants or subsidies.
The evidence does not establish that the payments were illegal.
The evidence does not establish that the payments were intended to keep Politico alive.
And the MS NOW rebranding was officially connected to the Comcast/Versant corporate separation, rather than a stated collapse in viewership or credibility.
There is nevertheless a legitimate separate question about whether federal agencies should have spent millions of taxpayer dollars on Politico Pro and other commercial information services, and whether individual contracts delivered sufficient value for money. That is a procurement/value-for-money question, rather than evidence by itself of an illegal subsidy or corruption.
Overall factual picture
Trump’s post contains genuine underlying facts — particularly the federal spending on Politico — but several of the explanations attached to those facts are unsupported or materially misleading.

Throughout his presidency, Trump has repeatedly urged television networks to cancel news or entertainment shows that he disapproves of or where he or his administration are ridiculed or criticized. He has also asked the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to revoke licenses from certain networks after criticizing their news coverage and other programming.
Last year, he excluded the Associated Press from the group of journalists covering his travels because the news agency did not adopt his preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico. Trump instructed federal employees to refer to it as the “Gulf of America.”
Additionally, the Pentagon attempted to introduce a new press policy that would limit journalists’ ability to obtain and report sensitive information. This initiative was abandoned after several media organizations refused to sign the commitment. Later, a federal judge ruled the new policy unconstitutional.
Trump has also initiated significant legal battles with major media outlets, including the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, CNN, ABC News, and BBC.
Reaction from CNN: “An Illegal Assault on a Fundamental Right”
CNN stated that while President Trump claimed the decision would take effect immediately, there were no indications that his administration was taking steps to implement it.
At the time of writing, CNN reporters remained at their posts within the White House, near the briefing room.
“CNN fully supports our White House team and their accurate reporting. Under the U.S. Constitution, we have the right to conduct these reports without obstruction or interference from the government,” the network declared in a statement.
They added, “If the ban President Trump threatens is enforced, it would represent an illegal assault on this fundamental right protected by the Constitution.”

sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AURN News) — President Donald Trump announced Friday in a Truth Social post that he is banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, accusing the outlets of spreading “fake news” and warning that more media organizations could be next.
The latest action adds to a growing series of disputes between Trump and major news organizations.
It follows an earlier legal fight with The Associated Press, which sued after the White House restricted its access to some presidential events over the news organization’s continued use of “Gulf of Mexico” rather than “Gulf of America.”
Paramount, CBS’ parent company, agreed to a $16 million settlement in Trump’s lawsuit over a “60 Minutes” interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. ABC News separately agreed to pay $15 million to settle Trump’s defamation lawsuit over comments made by George Stephanopoulos.
Trump is also pursuing lawsuits against The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal, while the FCC has opened investigations or proceedings involving ABC, NBC, PBS and NPR during Trump’s second term.
The White House has not clarified whether the ban applies to press credentials, access to specific events or something broader.

Trump defends banning CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House: ‘I don’t think a court should allow fake news’
At an Oval Office event to promote changes he says he’s making to the US healthcare system, including pressing for lower drug prices and reducing vaccine doses for children, Donald Trump defended his decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House.
Reminded by one correspondent that every president takes an oath to uphold the constitution, including the first amendment right to free speech, the president said, “you get so tired of reading and seeing fake news.”
“There may be others to join them,” Trump warned, before hinting that the New York Times and the Washington Post are on his list.
When another reporter reminded Trump that he had lost in court in 2018 when he tried to ban CNN’s Jim Acosta from the White House, Trump tried to rewrite history by claiming that “we didn’t have to take it too far because the reporter that you’re talking about discredited himself.” In fact, after a judge ordered the White House to restore Acosta’s access, the first Trump administration relented immediately.
“I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day,” Trump went on. “I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they’re going to write false stories all the time,” he insisted, apparently failing to understand a fundamental part of the US constitution.
Trump then went on to reveal that what he is mainly upset about is the tenor of coverage of him not being positive enough from non-partisan media outlets, while praising partisan, rightwing outlets.
“I get I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox,” Trump said. “But what I do ask is just a semblance of truth.”

Here is a statement from Jameel Jaffer, the executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, on Donald Trump’s move to bar CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House for unflattering coverage of his work as president:
 The First Amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he doesn’t like their coverage, just as it prohibits him from punishing universities because he doesn’t like the courses they offer, or from punishing law firms because he doesn’t like the clients they represent. With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you’d think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now. If President Trump means to expel these news organizations from the White House press pool, his action is doubly unconstitutional because the press pool is a ‘public forum’ under the First Amendment, which means the president can’t exclude journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints.
“Donald Trump just did what dictators throughout history have done,” Chuck Schumer, the leader of the Senate Democrats posted in response to Trump’s move to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House.
Directly addressing Trump on social media, Schumer added: “this is a democracy. You will not be able to manipulate the news or hide the truth.”
Trump says that his son paid back Kremlin-linked Russian who covered wedding party costs
Asked by a reporter in the Oval Office on Friday if it was appropriate for Umar Kremlev, a Russian linked to the Kremlin, to have paid for part of Donald Trump Jr’s wedding celebration in the Bahamas, Donald Trump said “it’s totally allowed. But as I understand it, he paid him back.”
“A person that he knows pretty, I guess a friend of his, gave him a wedding party. That’s very common, I’ve heard of many people giving wedding parties,” Trump added.
When the reporter seemed to suggest that a Putin-connected boxing official was not just a routine friend to make such a gift, Trump replied: “Well, I don’t know, maybe he didn’t do a background check. But I’ve given wedding parties to numerous people.”
“With all of that being said, I understand that Don’s paid him back,” Trump added.
Trump defends banning CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House: ‘I don’t think a court should allow fake news’
At an Oval Office event to promote changes he says he’s making to the US healthcare system, including pressing for lower drug prices and reducing vaccine doses for children, Donald Trump defended his decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House.
Reminded by one correspondent that every president takes an oath to uphold the constitution, including the first amendment right to free speech, the president said, “you get so tired of reading and seeing fake news.”
“There may be others to join them,” Trump warned, before hinting that the New York Times and the Washington Post are on his list.
When another reporter reminded Trump that he had lost in court in 2018 when he tried to ban CNN’s Jim Acosta from the White House, Trump tried to rewrite history by claiming that “we didn’t have to take it too far because the reporter that you’re talking about discredited himself.” In fact, after a judge ordered the White House to restore Acosta’s access, the first Trump administration relented immediately.
“I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day,” Trump went on. “I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they’re going to write false stories all the time,” he insisted, apparently failing to understand a fundamental part of the US constitution.
Trump then went on to reveal that what he is mainly upset about is the tenor of coverage of him not being positive enough from non-partisan media outlets, while praising partisan, rightwing outlets.
“I get I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox,” Trump said. “But what I do ask is just a semblance of truth.”
Journalists, lawmakers attack Trump’s order to block news outlets from White House
A flurry of journalists and Democratic lawmakers took to social media to criticize Donald Trump’s plan to bar several news outlets from the White House (also announced over social media).
“This is yet another attack on the First Amendment from a president who knows he and his party of bootlickers are deeply unpopular,” JB Pritzker, the governor of Illinois and potential 2028 presidential contender, posted on X after the announcement. “Donald Trump can’t hide from his failing record, so he’s banning journalists he doesn’t like to keep you from hearing about it.”
The president posted earlier this afternoon that he intended to bar three outlets – Politico, CNN and MS Now – from the White House, alleging that they reported “FICTION and LIES”. He threatened to do the same to other outlets peddling “fake news”.
Ruben Gallego, a Democratic senator from Arizona, called the ban “straight out of the authoritarian playbook”.
Trump doubled down on the ban while addressing reporters in the Oval Office on Friday.
“Because they’re fake news”, Trump said, when asked why he wanted to block the outlets’ access. “You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news. When you look at CNN, it’s just fake.”
“There may be others to join them,” Trump added.

Trump says he has banned CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House
In a new post to his personal social media platform, Donald Trump said that he would ban three news outlets – CNN, MS Now (formerly MSNBC) and Politico – from the White House.
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” the US president wrote.
Trump threatened that other media outlets were soon to face the same punishment. What exactly prompted the president to ax those three outlets – beyond familiar allegations that they were “fake news” – was not immediately clear. Nor did he elaborate on which outlets he would consider targeting.
